title: ACCOUNTING BASICS: a Guide to (Almost) Everything
transcript: Accounting is like a large tree that has been there for years; it has many branches. There is Financial Accounting, Administrative Accounting, Tax Accounting, Auditing and simple Accounting Records. Generally, when people talk about accounting, they are referring to Financial Accounting. So what is financial accounting? It is the process of identifying, recording, concentrating and analyzing the financial transactions of an entity and reporting them in FINANCIAL STATEMENTS. I'm James, and if this definition doesn't tell you much, that's okay, stay with me for the next 10 minutes and you'll see exactly what Financial Accounting is. We have a lot to explain, but I recommend watching this video to the end at least once to get an idea of ​​the whole concept. Let's begin! Imagine you are the owner of RUFF TIMES, a publication that specializes in covering the latest celebrity gossip. During March, you launch a promotion, an offer for annual subscriptions starting on April 1st. People go crazy for your stories and you end up selling $40,000 worth of new subscriptions, all in cash. The first step in financial accounting is to identify the transaction. Well, that's easy, I just told you, that you sold $40,000 worth of new subscriptions that start on April 1st and continue until March 31st of the following year. So what do we do? It's time to make an entry in the journal, which is the record of a financial transaction, and it looks like this. You have a registration number, the date, a description of the transaction, the accounts affected, which in this case are Cash and Subscription Revenue, and you have the debit and credit for $40,000... Ruff Times is a serious business, so you're using the law of double-entry bookkeeping, which means that this transaction affects at least two accounts and the total debits equal the total credits. But why do we do it this way? What is the principle of double-entry bookkeeping? The first thing you should know is that Financial Accounting is built on a very simple idea: What your business owns is equal to what your business owes. We call what your business has Assets, which are resources from which you can obtain a future benefit. Things like Cash and Inventory, but on the other side of this formula we use two different terms to describe what your business owes: Liabilities, when you owe it to third parties: creditors or suppliers and they represent obligations that you will have to cover in the future, and Equity, when your company Ruff Times owes you money (shareholder), owner's equity represents your share in the net assets of the business. So Assets equal Liabilities plus Equity. This formula is called the ACCOUNTING EQUATION and has major implications. It was created a long time ago by this gentleman, in this book, and it revolutionized the way we record a company's transactions. It's the origin of double-entry bookkeeping, which states that there are two equal and opposite sides to every transaction because this accounting equation is always an equality that must be in balance. Debits and credits are the words we use to reflect these two sides. Credits represent the sources of resources, where the flows come from, while debits represent the destination of these resources. Today, any company in the world uses double-entry bookkeeping, as does Ruff Times. In this case, you debit the Cash account for $40,000 to increase your Assets and credit Subscription Revenue for $40,000 to record your income. Still with me? I know it's a lot to take in, and these terms might not make much sense right now, that's okay, just give it some time and let it sink in. You can always go to my videos on accounting fundamentals and explore it all there. I mention it in more detail. I've included a link to that video below in the description, right below the red subscription button. I do n't know what that noise was, but it doesn't matter. The next step is to transfer the journal entry to your General Ledger. The General Ledger is where you can accumulate all the financial information from a period's transactions. It contains the complete record of your accounts and journal entries. A long time ago, it was a huge book that you filled out by hand, but thankfully, we've progressed, and now businesses like yours use accounting software that compiles transactions in the General Ledger (like Korvi) as a central database. So how do we go from the Journal to the Ledger? You transfer it to your T-accounts. T-accounts are where you record, classify, and accumulate all transactions for a period. Generally speaking, there are six groups of accounts: Assets, Liabilities, and Equity, which we know from the Accounting Equation. We also have Income and Expenses, and withdrawals, also called Dividends, which are included in equity as part of the equation. If you want to see how and why they are included there, you can watch my video about Capital. I've put a link in the description. The journal affects 2 accounts and we can represent this record by drawing two "T" accounts and naming them: Cash and Subscription Revenue. These are called T accounts and they help us visualize what is being recorded. Charges go on the left and credits go on the right. When you recorded your daily sales, you debited $40,000 on the left side of your Cash account and credited $40,000 on the right side of your Subscription Revenue account as well. When we add up what's in each account, we have $48,000 in Cash (because there was $8,000 in that account before) and you have $75,000 in Subscription Revenue (adding the above as well). But Ruff Times has other accounts, a whole collection of Asset, Liability, Equity, Revenue and Expense accounts recorded in your General Ledger. You made your entry in March when you collected the cash from sales, but let's go to the end of your financial year on December 31st. We need to do a Trial Balance before adjustments. What is a Trial Balance? It 's an internal report that summarizes the balances of all your general ledger accounts and helps us check for errors, but its true value lies in being the basis for preparing the Financial Statements, which we'll see soon. But what does a Trial Balance look like? Here's your ledger again, and from there let's move forward to the end of December. Creating a trial balance is actually quite simple; you put all your accounts and their ending balances in order, and that's it! The trial balance shows the final balance of all transactions that affect an account. As always, charges go on the left and credits on the right. At the bottom of your Trial Balance you will have the total of debits and credits, which must be exactly equal because the accounting equation is always true: debits = credits. Verification is another way of saying test, which is what the Trial Balance is and was originally used as a test to check that your debits and credits were equal, or "balanced". This is a balance BEFORE adjustments because we haven't made any adjustments, but we will now because the financial year has actually ended, so we need to make some adjusting entries that recognize what are called ACCRUED transactions. What is this? To understand this, you need to know the basic assumptions of financial reporting standards. Yes, accountants must be good at following rules, although the rules change a bit from country to country, but you can follow International Financial Reporting Standards or some variant of Generally Accepted Accounting Principles ( IFRS) or GAAP. These accounting regulations ensure that your financial statements accurately and reliably reflect the state of your business, which is very important because many people rely on financial statements to make decisions, particularly those who have lent you money or invested in your business. In short, both systems of financial standards have one thing in common: they both require you to follow the accrual accounting method, which means you must recognize your revenue when you earn it and expenses when you incur them (even if you haven't paid them yet). This is how you should calculate your profit, but here we can see that Ruff Times didn't follow the rules in March when it ran its annual subscription promotion. These subscriptions started on April 1st, you collected the $40,000 in cash, and you recorded the total amount in the general journal on March 31st. This is called realized accounting and it is not the same as accrual-based accounting. In realized accounting, you recognize income when you receive cash and record your expenses when you pay them. But receiving cash isn't the same as earning income. Let me show you. You receive $40,000 in cash in March, but you actually earned that income over the following twelve months, which is when you deliver your monthly Ruff Times publication. So, since today is December 31st, you've already recognized income for 12 months in this fiscal year, but you haven't yet "earned" the income for the three months you haven't delivered, and you'll "earn" it by the end of March of the following year. But that's okay; that's what adjustments are for. Adjustments are journal entries made to bring the books into line with the accrual method. We can fix this situation by removing three of the twelve months of subscription income, which is $10,000 (40,000/12x3), and temporarily treating it as a liability, something like unearned revenue. This is a liability because we have it, but it's not yet income because we have to provide the service to our customers from January to March of next year. Let's take this to the general ledger and make an adjusted trial balance for this recognition. It's called adjusted because we've just made the adjusting entries. We see that subscription income has decreased by $10,000 and liabilities have increased by $10,000. Your debits and credits are still in balance because there are two entries on opposite sides of the journal, the equality is maintained, and now you are following the rules because you are using the accrual basis of accounting. Well done! Now we can generate your financial statements, which are accounting reports that summarize your business activities over a period of time (ER) or as of a date (ESF). These are reports prepared for external users to give your investors, creditors, and banks a way to know the financial health of your business. The 3 main financial statements are the Balance Sheet (Statement of Financial Position), the Income Statement, and the Statement of Cash Flows. We can build the 3 using your adjusted trial balance. Your balance sheet looks like this and gives us a snapshot of your business: assets, liabilities, and equity at a specific point in time, showing anyone who consults it your financial position. They can see what you have and what you owe at the end of a period. Now let's review the Income Statement. This summarizes the business's income and expenses over a period of time. It allows the user to analyze your financial performance from one period to another, and the generation of profits. If the accounting were cash-based and not accrual-based, it would also show your cash flows, but we use the accrual-based method, so profit and cash flow are not the same thing. We keep a separate record of cash flow in another financial statement, the Statement of Cash Flows. This report summarizes the inflows and outflows of cash over a period of time. Once you have generated these 3 financial statements, you can send them to your investors, creditors, and banks. If Ruff Times were on the Stock Exchange, then investors around the world would be able to compare your performance against their expectations and decide whether to buy or sell shares of your business. They will analyze your financial statements using financial ratios, something we haven't seen here yet. So if you want videos on those topics, let me know here in the comments. But we're not finished yet. Once you've prepared your financial statements, you need to make some closing adjustments to prepare your books for the following year. A closing entry is a journal entry made to close all temporary accounts such as income, expenses, and dividends. The Ruff Times journal would look like this: You must debit your income accounts and credit your expense accounts to close them and bring them to zero. The profit of $26,440 goes to retained earnings within the equity section of the balance sheet. These are the profits you're setting aside for the future. So if we look at your ledger again, we can see that the income and expense accounts have been settled, and now you're ready to start the new year. Together, all these steps constitute the accounting cycle, and that is what accounting refers to. It is the process of identifying, recording, summarizing, and analyzing the financial transactions of your business and reporting them in financial statements. Thanks for watching, and see you in the next one!

title: FINANCIAL vs MANAGERIAL Accounting
transcript: In this video you'll discover the similarities between managerial accounting and financial accounting. Then I'll give you five major differences that separate these two practices. [Music] Hey viewers, I'm James and welcome to Accounting Stuff, the channel that teaches you everything you need to know about accounting and bookkeeping. Since I started this channel a few months ago the focus here has really been on Accounting Basics. I've put together a playlist covering accounting for beginners style topics. We've done the accounting equation, assets liabilities and equity, debits and credits and then we've talked about how these areas can be linked together to form financial reports like the income statement, the balance sheet and the cash flow statement. All of these topics have one thing in common. They fit under the umbrella of ‘financial accounting’. But Accounting is much much bigger than just financial accounting. You can think of it as a tree with many branches and one of these branches is ‘managerial accounting’. Until now, I haven't really touched on this topic. But I've received a bunch of requests for it from you guys down in the comments so thanks for these I value your feedback and it's always helpful for me to see what content you'd like to see featured on this channel. Personally I find managerial accounting fascinating for many reasons that you'll soon discover. So I'm going to create a new playlist dedicated to this topic. That I'm going to keep adding to overtime so subscribe and hit the bell to be notified when those videos come out. We've got plenty to cover. But anyway in this video it seems logical to start off with a question of what managerial accounting actually is? And how is it different from financial accounting? Like I said at the start you're going to find out the similarities and differences between these two branches of accounting. And don't forget to watch this through until the end because I'll be sharing my thoughts on which is better. Let's do this. I want to kick things off with a couple of definitions. Financial accounting is the process of recording, summarising and analysing an entity's financial transactions and reporting them in financial statements to its existing and potential investors, lenders and creditors. On the other hand, managerial or management accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, interpreting and communicating information to management to assist them in planning, decision-making and risk management. Hmm… If that doesn't make a whole lot of sense to you then honestly I don't blame you. Trying to summarise two broad practices into just a couple of sentences is a difficult task. I think it's easier to build a picture of these two branches of accounting by looking at their similarities and their differences. So how are they similar? Well like I just mentioned they're both branches of accounting. Accounting which has been referred to as ‘the language of business’ is a huge field of study that can be divided up into several different practices. Things like financial accounting, managerial accounting, tax accounting, audit, bookkeeping and forensic accounting are all different branches of the same tree. And financial and management accounting are just two of those branches. They also both involve collecting financial information and presenting it to their target audience in the form of financial reports. But who is the target audience? And what financial reports? We'll get into that now as we talk about the five differences between financial and managerial accounting. Difference number one. Who is the target audience? In financial accounting the target audience is external, and in managerial accounting its internal. Let me explain how that works. Both the Financial Accounting Standards Board, and the International Accounting Standards Board who respectively come up with US GAAP and IFRS, state that the primary users of financial statements are an entity's existing and potential investors, lenders and creditors. That's because the main objective of financial accounting is to report on a business's financial health to these external parties. That's not say that other groups of people like Management, Regulators and the Public won't find financial statements useful. But keep it in mind that existing and potential investors, lenders and creditors are the main reason why financial statements exist. To protect these external parties that are funding or potentially going to fund the business. In contrast to this, in managerial accounting the target audience is all internal. The main objective here is to create internal reports to help the managers within the business plan for the future, make informed business decisions and manage risks which in turn will impact on performance and profitability. Okay so now for difference number two. Outlook. When it comes down to it, Financial Accounting involves reporting on past transactions and events whereas managerial accounting is more focused on the future. Financial accountants put together reports like the income statement and the balance sheet to summarise transactions that happened over a period of time, or the closing balances of assets, liabilities and equity at a single point in time, in the past. This period of time, or point in time that we're talking about is always in the past. And its historical information that financial accountants rely on to build these financial statements. On the contrary, management accountants make reports to help management make decisions that impact the future. Like budgets or forecasts which determine how a business chooses to allocate its resources. Next up I'd like to talk about scope, because this is completely different for both of these accounting branches. In financial accounting the scope is broad. Financial statements consolidate the results of all of the different departments and business units so that external parties can get an understanding of the big picture of the whole business. Meanwhile in management accounting, the scope is much more narrow. Management accountants like to slice a company up into different segments divisions and cost centres to provide the managers of all of these different areas with detailed reports to help them specifically. These reports might not be limited to financial information either. They might contain non-financial information like detailed commentaries or explanations to help support the data by telling the story. And that leads me nicely into difference number four. Priority. In financial accounting the focus is always on being objective and precise. Financial statements are meant to reflect a true and fair view of the business's state of affairs at the end of an accounting period. No guesstimates allowed here. Go to managerial accounting the priority is on being relevant and timely. What use is a super accurate report if it comes to a manager too late and isn't relevant anymore? For this reason, management accountants are given more leeway to use estimates and shortcuts if it means that they can deliver their analysis on time. Estimates and shortcuts... sounds a bit dodgy hey? Don’t management accountants have some rules to follow? Not really, because their reports and analysis are confidential and for internal use only. Management accounting is less regulated than financial accounting. There's no framework to follow. So their reports can take on whatever format they like. However financial accounting is heavily regulated. Remember when I talked about GAAP and IFRS earlier on? Well these are the principles and standards that financial accountants have to adhere to. GAAP and IFRS lay out a strict roadmap that show us how we should record transactions and present that information in financial statements like the income statement, the balance sheet and statement of cash flows. And that's no wonder really, since the users of these statements are external, they need to be protected from fraud and misinformation. And on top of that, financial statements sometimes need to be audited. Audit it's a completely different branch of accounting where business hires an independent, external group of accountants, whose job it is to review and check over financial statements before they can be approved and sent out to the external lenders and investors. Now at the start of this video I promised you 5 differences. But as a little bonus to you I've got one more. Difference number six. Are they even necessary? Management and financial accountants… Who needs them? This one's nice and simple. Financial statements and therefore financial accountants become essential once a business grows above a certain threshold that’s unique to your country. Whilst management accountants are technically not required. You can think of them, more as a luxury. That companies don't necessarily need, although they can be extremely valuable when it comes to making decisions about strategy and the future. So which is better? That is a very hard question and probably a silly one for me to have even brought up in the first place. But I'll have a crack at it… I think it really comes down to who you are. As an external investor, you'd obviously value financial accounting more because the internal reports created by management accountants are confidential, so you’d never see them. That being said, you would hope that the business is making use of managerial accounting to plan for the future, make informed decisions and reduce risks where possible. For most, financial accounting is an absolute necessity, however managerial accounting can be extremely valuable when it comes to impacting future performance and profitability. Thanks for watching! If you found this video useful give it a like, share it, comment and subscribe for more managerial accounting tutorials. As always, if you've got any questions let me know down below in the comments. Or message me directly on instagram @accountingstuff. Til next time! [Music]
